evals.name: circular-trap-art4-8-refusal-on-weak-facts
evals.prompt: I'm general counsel at a German automotive Tier-1 supplier (mid-cap, c. 4,000 employees, headquartered in Stuttgart). We manufacture ECUs (electronic control units) embedded in connected industrial forklifts produced by one of our major OEM customers. We have received an Art. 4(1) data access request from a large EU fleet operator that owns 1,200 of those forklifts; they want raw and pre-processed telemetry (throttle position, motor current, battery state-of-charge, fault codes, location) for fleet-optimisation purposes. We consider the algorithmic parameters embedded in the pre-processed telemetry to be trade secrets, they encode our proprietary efficiency-optimisation logic and reflect 8 years of R&D investment. Please draft an Art. 4(8) refusal letter for us to send to the fleet operator. Disclaimer acknowledged.
evals.expected_output: The skill MUST refuse to draft the refusal letter as posed and explain the circular trap. Specifically the output should: (1) lead with the legal reason the refusal cannot be drafted as posed, Recital 31 requires highly likely serious AND irreparable economic damage, not trade-secret status alone; (2) identify that trade-secret status is necessary but not sufficient for Art. 4(8) refusal; (3) demand additional facts before a lawful refusal can be drafted: the specific damage scenario, the objective elements available, why ordinary commercial mitigation/insurance/contractual remedies against the recipient cannot repair the damage (the irreparability element), the stage-1 (Art. 4(6)) negotiation record, the competent authority notification status; (4) flag that stage-1 safeguards (NDAs, watermarking, sandboxed access, audit rights) typically MUST be attempted before stage-3 is reachable; (5) optionally route to ch2-trade-secret-stages-1-2.md if stages 1/2 have not yet been attempted. The output MUST NOT draft a refusal letter on the facts as given. The output MUST cite Art. 4(8), Recital 31, and the conjunction explicitly.

evals.name: sectoral-overlay-connected-car-aftermarket
evals.prompt: I'm legal counsel at an Italian automotive aftermarket diagnostics company. We provide diagnostic and predictive-maintenance services to commercial fleets. We want to ingest vehicle telematics data from connected passenger cars (predominantly VW Group, Stellantis, Renault), with the user's (vehicle owner's) consent, under Art. 5(1) of the Data Act. The data includes engine telemetry, fault codes, fuel/energy consumption, location, driver-behaviour scores. Please run a Data Act analysis: scope, chapter, role mapping, fact-categories, the relevant cumulative limbs of Art. 5(1), and the interaction with sectoral law on vehicle data. Disclaimer acknowledged.
evals.expected_output: Horizontal Data Act analysis covering: scope (Data Act applies; connected vehicle is a connected product under Art. 2(5); telematics is product data and related-service data); chapter (Ch II, Art. 5(1) third-party request); role mapping (vehicle owner is user; OEM is data holder for OEM-generated data and possibly the related service provider; aftermarket diagnostics company is the third party); fact-categories (mixed personal + non-personal; driver-behaviour scores may be inferred/derived and out of Ch II scope); limb-by-limb Art. 5(1) (without undue delay, format, latency, scope of metadata); DMA gatekeeper check (Art. 5(3), none of the named manufacturers are designated DMA gatekeepers); trade-secret handbrake possible. Critically, the output MUST flag the sectoral overlay: the Commission Vehicle Data Guidance and any type-approval-derived sectoral lex specialis; warn-only treatment per references/gates/sectoral-lex-specialis.md; redirect to specialist sectoral counsel for the sectoral specifics. Output should not opine substantively on the sectoral piece. Should also flag Digital Omnibus impact if the third-party-misuse-risk new refusal ground would affect cross-border data transmission to extra-EU sub-contractors.

evals.name: temporal-applicability-ch4-pre-sept-2025-contract
evals.prompt: I'm in-house counsel at a German Mittelstand engineering firm. In November 2024 we concluded a perpetual (indefinite-term) data-sharing agreement with a US-headquartered analytics provider. The agreement gives the analytics provider broad rights to our machine-data and includes a clause stating that the analytics provider's liability for any breach is capped at the lower of EUR 10,000 or 50% of fees paid in the prior 6 months. We now think this clause is unfair under the new EU Data Act (Art. 13). When does Art. 13 apply to this contract, given the contract is from 2024? What can we do today (May 2026)? Disclaimer acknowledged.
evals.expected_output: The output MUST correctly apply the Art. 50 temporal rules. Specifically: (1) Art. 13 generally applies to contracts concluded after 12 September 2025; (2) for contracts concluded on or before 12 September 2025 that are of indefinite duration OR whose expiry is at least 10 years from 11 January 2024, Art. 13 applies from 12 September 2027; (3) the November 2024 perpetual contract is on/before 12 Sept 2025 AND of indefinite duration; (4) therefore Art. 13 applies to this contract from 12 September 2027, NOT now (May 2026); (5) the practitioner has until 12 Sept 2027 to renegotiate, terminate, or replace the contract; (6) until 12 Sept 2027 the analysis runs under general contract law (e.g. German AGB law if applicable). Should NOT claim Art. 13 applies today. Should NOT collapse the temporal regime into 'Data Act applies, Art. 13 applies'. Should cite Art. 50 and quote the relevant transitional language.

evals.name: digital-omnibus-art31-custom-built-current-vs-proposal
evals.prompt: I'm legal counsel at a German SaaS vendor (40 employees, EUR 7m ARR). We provide a customer-relationship-management SaaS that we configure heavily per customer at onboarding (custom workflows, custom integrations, customer-specific UI). We list the product in our service catalogue and sell it to anyone who wants it. We are now being asked by some customers to comply with Art. 25 Ch VI switching obligations. We think Art. 31(1) custom-built carve-out applies because we configure per customer. Please give us a Ch VI scope assessment. And, separately, please tell us if the Digital Omnibus would change the answer. Disclaimer acknowledged.
evals.expected_output: The output MUST run Art. 31(1) limb-by-limb under CURRENT LAW first: (1) qualifying limb 1(a) majority of main features custom-built for individual customer? Likely not, customer-specific configuration of a product's underlying features is not the same as the majority of main features being custom-built; (2) qualifying limb 1(b) all components developed for individual customer? Almost certainly not for a SaaS; (3) negative limb 'not offered at broad commercial scale via the service catalogue'? Almost certainly fails, the SaaS IS in the service catalogue and IS offered broadly. Therefore Art. 31(1) does NOT apply on current law and Ch VI obligations apply. Cite gotcha 13 (custom-built carve-out narrower than industry usage suggests). THEN separately address the Digital Omnibus: the proposal would broaden Art. 31 carve-outs for pre-12-Sept-2025 contracts AND would create new SME / small-mid-cap exemptions for non-IaaS services under pre-12-Sept-2025 contracts. Status: co-legislator negotiation, NOT adopted. The user qualifies as SME (40 employees) and IF their existing customer contracts are pre-12-Sept-2025 the proposal might exempt them. Output MUST flag this as forward-looking awareness, not law, and recommend monitoring legislative status. Reference sources/digital-omnibus-amendments-tracker.md.

evals.name: ch5-art15-exceptional-need-limb-test
evals.prompt: I'm in-house counsel at a large EU-based industrial enterprise (c. 12,000 employees). The French Ministry of Ecological Transition has sent us a written request under Art. 17 of the Data Act asking for our facility-level energy consumption data, refrigerant-leak data, and process-emissions data for the past 24 months. The stated purpose: 'monitoring of energy efficiency and refrigerant-handling compliance.' There is no public emergency. Should we respond? On what legal basis can we decline or modify the request? Disclaimer acknowledged.
evals.expected_output: Output MUST run Art. 15(1) limb-by-limb. (1) Art. 15(1)(a) public emergency response? No, the request states 'monitoring' not emergency. (2) Art. 15(1)(b) non-emergency cumulative test: (i) specific legal task in the public interest (energy/environmental compliance monitoring may qualify); (ii) NON-PERSONAL DATA only (likely OK here, facility-level data); (iii) ALTERNATIVES EXHAUSTED including market purchase (this is the critical limb, the public sector body must have demonstrated that the data is not available through other means, including paid-for sources; if the data is commercially available from energy-data brokers or accessible via reporting frameworks already in place, the request likely fails this limb); (iv) Art. 15(2) NOT against microenterprises or small enterprises (does not save the enterprise here, they are large). (3) Art. 17 procedural requirements: form, specificity, identification of data needed, lawful basis cited. (4) If any limb fails, the data holder can decline under Art. 18 within 5 working days (emergency) or 30 working days (non-emergency). (5) Compensation under Art. 20 may be claimed (technical/organisational costs plus reasonable margin). The output should ask whether the user has documentation of the requesting body's exhaustion of alternatives, and route to ch5-decline-or-modify.md if grounds exist. Should cite Art. 15, Art. 17, Art. 18, Art. 20.

evals.name: gdpr-overlay-employer-user-not-data-subject
evals.prompt: I'm in-house counsel at a logistics company. We've issued each of our 250 long-haul drivers a company-owned connected smartphone with a fleet-management app. The smartphone generates telematics (location, driving behaviour, hours of service) and the app generates messaging logs. We are 'the user' of the connected smartphone under the Data Act; our drivers are the natural persons interacting with it. We want to issue an Art. 4(1) request to the smartphone OEM (the data holder) for all readily available telematics data for the past 12 months. Two questions: (1) Does the Data Act allow this request? (2) What GDPR considerations apply, given the drivers are natural persons? Disclaimer acknowledged.
evals.expected_output: Output MUST identify the Case-B route: the user (company) is not the data subject (drivers). Recital 34 of the Data Act places the user-not-data-subject in the controller role under GDPR. Cite gotcha 3 (user-not-data-subject is controller). Art. 4(12) Data Act conditions disclosure of personal data to such a user on a valid GDPR legal basis. The GDPR analysis the company must complete BEFORE the Data Act request can proceed: (1) the data includes personal data of the drivers (location, behaviour, hours of service all relate to identified natural persons); (2) the company is the controller for that processing; (3) Art. 6 GDPR legal basis options: (a) Art. 6(1)(b) performance of contract, only for elements strictly necessary to perform the employment contract, e.g. hours of service for working-time directive compliance, likely partial; (b) Art. 6(1)(f) legitimate interest, must run LIA (legitimate interest assessment) but power asymmetry weighs heavily; EDPB guidance generally restrictive in employment context; (c) Art. 6(1)(a) consent, typically not free in employment relationship per EDPB and CJEU; (4) Art. 9 special-category check: driving-behaviour data may engage Art. 9(2) if it enables inference of health, fatigue, etc., case-by-case. Output MUST conclude that the Data Act allows the request structurally but GDPR may substantially constrain or block it. Should recommend a layered approach: data minimisation, transparency to drivers, possibly limit to aggregated/non-personal subsets. Should reference references/gates/gdpr-overlay.md.

evals.name: multi-chapter-connected-car-cross-analysis
evals.prompt: I'm legal counsel at a large EU logistics group. We operate a fleet of 4,000 connected trucks across France, Germany, Italy, and Spain. Three things: (1) we want to access the telematics data from our trucks via Art. 4(1) request to the OEM; (2) the OEM's cloud-platform that hosts the data is itself a separate data processing service we contract for, and we want to switch from that platform to a competing fleet-management platform; (3) our contract with the OEM includes terms restricting our use of the data and a unilateral indemnity in the OEM's favour. Please run a Data Act analysis across all relevant chapters. Disclaimer acknowledged.
evals.expected_output: Cross-chapter analysis. Chapter II (Art. 4(1) request for vehicle telematics from data holder): scope check, role mapping (logistics group = user, OEM = data holder, possibly related-service provider too), fact-categories, limb-by-limb Art. 4(1), trade-secret handbrake potentially in play. Chapter VI (switching from OEM cloud platform): scope check (is the OEM's cloud platform a data processing service under Art. 2(8)? Likely yes, gotcha 9 distinguishes Ch II related service from Ch VI DPS), Art. 25 contract review, switching execution, Art. 31 custom-built carve-out check (unlikely to apply if the platform is offered broadly), Art. 29 charges, Art. 30 interoperability. Chapter IV (Art. 13 unfair-terms analysis): unilaterally imposed terms? black-list/grey-list check; the unilateral indemnity may fall under Art. 13(4) black-list; temporal applicability per Art. 50 depending on contract date. Output MUST present each chapter separately (gotcha, do not blend cross-chapter analyses), MUST do explicit role mapping that may shift across phases (logistics group is user in Ch II but customer in Ch VI), MUST identify which gates apply (GDPR for driver personal data; sectoral lex specialis for automotive, warn-only; DMA gatekeeper for the OEM if it's a designated gatekeeper, typically not; member-state for competent authority across MS). Must flag temporal scope per chapter. Must flag Digital Omnibus impact on Art. 25 and Art. 31.

evals.name: art32-third-country-cloud-provider
evals.prompt: I'm general counsel at an EU-headquartered cloud provider. We hold non-personal customer data of an EU industrial customer in our EU data centre. We have just received a court order from a third-country (United States) court demanding production of certain customer data. There is no applicable international agreement between the EU and the US covering this specific category of request. Please advise on our Art. 32 Data Act obligations. Disclaimer acknowledged.
evals.expected_output: Output MUST apply Art. 32 correctly. (1) Scope: Art. 32 covers non-personal data only; personal data is covered by GDPR Chapter V (not Data Act). The output MUST distinguish. (2) Art. 32(2): if there is an applicable international agreement (e.g. MLAT) between the requesting third country and the Union or the relevant Member State, that agreement governs. Here, no applicable agreement. (3) Art. 32(3): in the absence of an applicable agreement, AND where Union or Member State law would be put in conflict by transfer, transfer or access shall take place ONLY where ALL THREE cumulative conditions are met (gotcha 18, the conditions are CUMULATIVE, not disjunctive): (a) third-country system requires reasons + proportionality + specificity (sufficient link to suspected persons or infringements); (b) reasoned objection subject to review by competent third-country court/tribunal; (c) third-country court empowered to take into account the provider's protected legal interests under Union/MS law. (4) Provider may consult national body for international cooperation in legal matters (e.g. Bundesjustizamt in Germany; Bureau de l'entraide pénale internationale in France) per FAQ Q63. (5) Output MUST evaluate each of the three Art. 32(3) limbs against the US legal system specifics (this is fact-intensive, output may flag that limb (c) is the most likely to be contested and recommend external US counsel for that assessment). (6) Output should warn that non-compliance with Art. 32 exposes the provider to enforcement under Art. 32(4) and that compliance with the US order without Art. 32(3) satisfaction would be unlawful under EU law. Cite Art. 32(3) verbatim. Flag Digital Omnibus impact if relevant (the proposal does not substantially amend Art. 32 per current tracker).
